name: Velvet Green
lede: Velvet Green is a muted yellow-green borrowing its name from [[velvet]], the fabric word, not from any green velvet in particular.

sections.title: A fabric word, not a hue family
sections.body: Maerz and Paul record Velvet Green as first appearing in 1902, on plate 22, chip L8, in their 1930 dictionary [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the chip as "moderate olive green," block 118 [1]. "Velvet" names a texture, not a color family, and the library's actual [[velvet]] is a dark magenta-purple, nowhere near this green — the shared word is coincidence, not kinship [2]. Our nearest named neighbor by measured color is [[military-green]], a slightly darker and more olive shade, with [[fern-green]] close behind [2]. A fourth near match, [[military-green]], is slightly duller still [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a match for Velvet Green in only 143 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.6 percent, more common than 54 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 11 of 1,674 paintings, 2.1 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive [3]. Camille Pissarro used it most: 5 of his 50 paintings here carry it, 6.6 times his peers' rate [3]. It is also most over-represented in French paintings generally, 2.6 times the expected rate [3]. The earliest archive match dates to 1500, four centuries before Maerz and Paul recorded the name, which again shows only a look-alike hue, not the dye or the word [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[3].
